case_name: Jewish Eldercare Centre v. J.H.H. Foundation-Fondation J.H.H.
text:
JM1838

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-05-067138-014

DATE:

November 4, 2002

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

ROBERT MONGEON, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

THE JEWISH ELDERCARE CENTRE

-and-

THE JEWISH ELDERCARE
FOUNDATION

Plaintiffs and
Cross-Defendants

Vs.

J.H.H. FOUNDATION-FONDATION
J.H.H.

-and-

MORRIS FREEDMAN

-and-

GERRY WEINSTEIN

-and-

MARTIN LABOW

-and-

TED SALONIN

Defendants and
Cross-Plaintiffs

______________________________________________________________________

J U
D G M E N T

______________________________________________________________________

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The parties to this litigation are institutions
and individuals which have one common objective:  the well being of the aging
population of the Jewish community.

[
2
]

Although there may be some differences of
opinions as to the ways and means of ensuring such well being, the Court wishes
to state, at the outset, that all parties and more particularly all individuals
involved in one capacity or another and who have been asked to testify, have
done so with a very high degree of probity, integrity and moral concern towards
the community they serve.  Consequently, the outcome of this case should not be
interpreted as the condemnation of some, or the victory of others.

[
3
]

Nevertheless, this litigation is the result of a
confrontation between two institutions and two groups of individuals who, over
the past thirty years or so, have devoted time resources and energy over the
proper care and treatment of their elders.  Through the efforts of all
concerned, the Jewish community was put to contribution to ensure that not only
proper  health care services would be offered or made available to the Jewish
aging population but also that non-subsidized (or "non shareable")
services would also continue to be offered, in line with the traditional
material and religious ways of life to which the Montreal Jewish community is
accustomed to offer and to receive.  Sometimes this confrontation has resulted
into harsh decisions and ultimatums.  Tough words were uttered and heard,
friendships were lost or perhaps irreconcilable enmities resulted.  But, in the
end, it is all for one common objective.

THE FACTS – THE PARTIES

[
4
]

The Jewish Hospital of Hope was incorporated in
1942.  For purposes of clarity, it will hereinafter be referred to as the
"Hospital".  Its primary dedication is the long term care treatment
and preservation of human dignity as well as the quality of life of its
patients.

[
5
]

The Jewish Nursing Home (the "Nursing
Home") is another well known institution of the Jewish community.  Its
principal function is to offer care and support to its elderly residents who
may show some degree of loss of autonomy but who are able to continue to
function and enjoy a better quality of life.  The Hospital will therefore look
after the short-term medical needs and treatments of its patients while the
Nursing Home will look after long-term assistance required by the convalescent
or elderly community.  The Nursing Home was incorporated in June 1973.

[
6
]

The J.H.H.  Foundation, a fund-raising
institution, was incorporated in 1972.  It will hereinafter be referred to as
the "Foundation".  Over the last three decades, its activities have
contributed to the financial well-being of the Hospital.  The Foundation is
very well known to all members of the Montreal Jewish community.  The
Foundation has been for the last thirty years, and still is, very active both
in its fund‑raising campaigns as well as in its support of various
activities and services, mainly towards the patients of  the Hospital and also
but to a lesser extent, for the benefit of  the residents of the Nursing Home.

[
7
]

The Jewish Nursing Home Foundation (the
"Nursing Home Foundation") is a fund‑raising institution for
the principal benefit of the Nursing Home.  It was incorporated in 1989.  Its
activities are not as well known.  Its support programs are not as developed as
those of the Foundation.

[
8
]

The Jewish Eldercare Centre is the result of the
impact of the Quebec health services reform of 1992.  Until then, the Hospital
and the Nursing Home were administered by two independent boards.  By 1994 the
Hospital and the Nursing Home were administered by a "Unified Board",
which will ultimately lead to the adoption of a plan of integration of all
medical and non‑medical services of the two establishments by the Régie
Régionale de la Santé et des Services Sociaux.   After several administrative
steps, the Hospital and the Nursing Home were in fact unified and integrated
into one administrative institution under the name "Jewish Eldercare
Centre‑CHSLD Juif de Montréal", hereinafter referred to as the
"Eldercare Centre".  The corporate recognition of the Eldercare
Centre came in 2001 although it had previously been ratified by its Unified
Board in the course of 2000.

[
9
]

For reasons which will become more apparent
later, the Nursing Home Foundation changed its name and became the Jewish
Eldercare Foundation (July  16,  2001) a few weeks after
supplementary letters‑patent created the Eldercare Centre (June 14,
2001).

[
10
]

As for the six individuals specifically named in
the action, they are the members of the Board of directors of the Foundation.
When referred to collectively, they will be identified as the
"Directors".

[
11
]

This case deals exclusively with one principal
issue:  control of fund‑raising and control of the funds generated by
such fund‑raising for the benefit of the Eldercare Centre, its patients
and residents.   The Eldercare Centre wishes to achieve this objective through
the conclusions sought by its action in permanent injunction.  The following
conclusions are directed against the Foundation and are summarized as follows:

a)

A prohibition from
using the name

"Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation" for any purpose.

b)

A prohibition from raising any funds
using
the name
of the Jewish Hospital of Hope or the Jewish Eldercare Centre.

c)

A prohibition from operating any gift shops or
coffee shops
under the name
of the Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation.

d)

A prohibition from
using or distributing any
monies
received for the benefit of the Hospital for any other purpose than
for the benefit of the Hospital.

e)

An order to
reimburse
to the Plaintiffs
all
funds received
in and for the Jewish Hospital of Hope or by the use of the
name of the Jewish Hospital of Hope.

(emphasis added)

[
12
]

The Eldercare Centre is also seeking a condemnation
against the Directors to pay exemplary damages in the amount of 100,000$.
[1]

[
13
]

To fully understand this whole matter, a review
of the principal facts is necessary.

THE FACTS – SOME HISTORICAL
BENCHMARKS

[
14
]

The Hospital was incorporated by special Act of
the Quebec Legislative Assembly on April 15, 1942 (exhibit P‑1).  The
creation of the Hospital was promoted by an organization known as the Hebrew
Consumptive Aid Association of Canada Inc., which had been active for some
thirty‑six years prior to 1942.  Following the donation of a important
tract of land by the City of Montreal and having raised the necessary funds,
the Jewish Hospital of Hope was built
[2]
.  Its
objects and purposes were set in exhibit P‑1 as follows
[3]
:

4.

The objects and purposes for which the
corporation is created by this act are:

a)

To operate, equip and maintain a hospital for
persons suffering from and afflicted with incurable diseases and/or any other
disease which may be determined by the by-laws of the said corporation and to
perform the functions and engage in the practices usually carried on by such a
hospital;

b)

The admission and care of persons, subject to
such limitations and charges as may be hereafter determined upon and settled by
the by-laws of the said corporation.

c)

The admission and care of such sick persons as
pauper patients, subject to such limitations and regulations as may be
determined by the said by-laws;

d)

To promote the surgical and medical sciences,
establish and develop laboratories for clinics, experimenting and scientific
research, or co-operate with any other corporation in establishing and
developing such laboratories for clinics, experimenting or scientific research,
and, subject to section 1 and following of chapter 265 of the Revised Statutes,
1941, respecting anatomy, to practise dissection on bodies for the instruction
of surgeons and physicians;

e)

The establishment or acquisition and the
carrying on of sanatoria for the treatment of tuberculosis and other diseases,
convalescent homes and nurses' residences and other institutions of a similar
nature.
[4]

[
15
]

During the period 1942 to 1972 the Hospital
accumulated substantial assets and reserves.  By 1972, its reserves were
approaching the two-million-dollar mark, a very substantial sum at the time.
Consequently when the Quebec health services reform of 1972 showed signs of
possible governmental appropriation of all assets, equipment and resources of
the Quebec public or private health institutions (including cash reserves or
other liquid assets), it was feared by the directors of the Hospital  that its
financial reserves could perhaps be at risk.  It was feared, more specifically,
that its accumulated reserves could be re-pooled and eventually re-distributed
not only for the benefit of the Hospital, its patients or the Jewish community,
but also for the benefit of all the population of Quebec.  This fear was so
strong that a group of individuals
[5]
decided
to constitute and incorporate a new entity, under the Canada Corporations Act,
and call it the J.H.H. Foundation in order to fully distinguish and segregate
it from the Hospital
[6]
.   This
way, it was perceived that the assets of the Foundation would be protected
against any possible appropriation by the Quebec government and would continue
to be available for the well-being of the Jewish elderly community.  The
Hospital then transferred to the Foundation, immediately after its inception,
an amount of nearly 1.8  million dollars (see exhibit P-5 which
refers to an amount of $1,799,284.16), in perpetuity.   No conditions were
attached to this transfer, not even the obligation, for the Foundation, to use
the capital or the interest generated therefrom for the benefit of the
Hospital.

[
16
]

There was also great care taken in ensuring that
the newly incorporated Foundation would not bear the full name, but only the
initials of, the Jewish Hospital of Hope.  This was arranged, once again, to
protect the Foundation from any direct or apparent connection between it and
the Hospital:  The Foundation did not have the same corporate name, it was not
incorporated under the laws of Quebec but, rather it was created under a
federal statute.  Its powers and objects were those generally given to a
charitable fund-raising foundation and no reference whatsoever was made to the
Hospital.  Furthermore, in the event of dissolution, its assets  (including the
1.8 million dollar transfer referred to above) are to be distributed to other
charitable organizations, in accordance with the general practice in such
matters, but not necessarily or exclusively, to the Hospital.  In point of
fact, the Foundation's charter does not make any reference to the Hospital.
The following portions of the Foundation' charter are noteworthy
[7]
:

The objects for which
incorporation of the proposed corporation is sought are:

a)

to promote and assist in charitable work in
Canada with particular emphasis in the territory encompassed by the Montreal
Urban Community in the Province of Quebec and particularly, but not as to
restrict the generality of the foregoing,
to provide the traditional Jewish
Community and others with funds for treatment, research, service and care of
chronic diseases, and those thereby affected
;

b)

to exclusively
in the name of the foundation
,

solicit
, and obtain gifts, legacies, and endowment
funds
in order
to
promote
the building, re‑building and expansion of charitable
institutions to carry on or presenting carrying on programmes of health,
welfare and educational services;

c)

to make gifts, grants, contributions, and
donations for charitable purposes to any charitable or scientific organization
or any other organization involved in health, welfare, educational services and
research which carries on its work solely within Canada;

d)

to do all such things as are incidental or
conducive to the attainment of the above objects.

The head office of the
Corporation will be situated in the territory of the Montreal Urban Community,
in the Province of Quebec.

Your applicants request that
it be ordained and declared that except to the extent that any special
conditions attaching thereto may otherwise provide, all gifts, donations,
bequests and subscriptions received by the Corporation shall be deemed to be
capital as opposed to income.

And your applicants
request that it be further ordained and declared that,
upon the dissolution
of the Corporation, and after payment of all debts and liabilities, the
remaining property of the Corporation shall be distributed or disposed of to
charitable organizations, preferably those interested in chronic diseases,
which carry on their work solely in Canada
.
[8]

(emphasis added)

[
17
]

Notwithstanding all these efforts made to
segregate, and even isolate, the Foundation from the Hospital, both
institutions were governed, managed and administered by the same persons,
sitting on two distinct boards of directors.   This obviously assured a common
direction to both institutions but this situation was never documented in a
resolution, contract or agreement
[9]
.

[
18
]

Further notwithstanding all the said efforts,
the Foundation quickly became known, in the everyday reality, as the
"Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation" rather than under its
abbreviated corporate name.   The evidence has overwhelmingly shown that,
within the community at large, the Foundation operated and was referred by that
name.

[
19
]

The full name Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation
was regularly used by the Hospital, by its staff, in communications with third
parties outside the Hospital or the Foundation, to the full knowledge of the
Hospital management and administration. It was never questioned, opposed, or in
any way, objected to.   In point of fact, the so-called "Chinese
Wall" which was erected between the Hospital and the Foundation in 1972
was for one purpose only:  to avoid the risk of losing control over substantial
cash resources resulting from donations from members of the Montreal Jewish
community as a whole.  Once this threat was gone, the "Chinese Wall"
sort of crumbled for lack of necessity and was not rebuilt, at least for the
time being.

[
20
]

This situation prevailed for as long as there
was a community of views and a community of interest between the Hospital and
the Foundation, i.e. for as long as the two institutions were administered by
the same people sitting on both boards of directors.   This is the situation
which prevailed at least until the inception of the first Unified Board  in
1994.

[
21
]

Parallel to the foregoing, the integration of
the Hospital and the Nursing Home started in 1994.  From 1994 to the end of
1997, matters progressed without any serious confrontations between the Unified
Board and the Foundation.

[
22
]

In the early part of 1998 the integration of the
Hospital and the Nursing Home under one single "unified board"
created new challenges and financial needs.  Certain sums were needed to
finance certain constructions, more particularly a covered passage between the
two buildings (the "Link" between the Hospital and the Nursing Home)
as well as certain new needs or services.  Some believed that the cost of the
Link should be absorbed at least in part by funds from the Foundation.  Some
others did not agree.  This was the beginning of the confrontation which will
ultimately culminate in the present legal proceedings.

[
23
]

In addition, the integration of the Hospital and
the Nursing Home has caused the abandonment of the name Jewish Hospital of Hope
in favour of the name Jewish Eldercare Centre, created to identify the
administrative regroupment of the Hospital (which remains for the time being
identified on the Hospital of Hope Pavilion
[10]

and of the Nursing Home which is now called the Kastner Pavilion
[11]
.  As a direct result of this regroupment,
it is however expected that the name Jewish Hospital of Hope, will, no longer
be used in connexion with the Eldercare Centre, its components or buildings.

[
24
]

As stated previously, over the period 1972 to
1998, the Foundation's use of the name Jewish Hospital of Hope was
overwhelming.  The use
by the Hospital
of the said name to describe or
identify the Foundation was also equally substantial.  The Court does not
intend to review all references to the Foundation as the Jewish Hospital of
Hope Foundation by various parties (including unrelated third parties, donors
testators, etc.) including the parties directly involved in this litigation.
Suffice it to say that the use of the said name was general and unfettered
[12]
.  Furthermore, such use was known to,
tolerated by and approved (if not expressly, at least implicitly),  by the
Plaintiffs.  In point of fact, the Hospital, then the Unified Board, had an
interest in holding the Foundation out as the Jewish Hospital of Hope
Foundation.

[
25
]

With the integration, came certain difficulties
and differences of opinion as to the use of the funds collected by the
Foundation.  It is not necessary or appropriate to review and discuss the
reasons or justifications invoked, or to determine who is right or wrong on the
various issues of concern or disagreements which arose.  Suffice it to say,
once again, that there were serious enough differences to ultimately create the
present confrontation over the presence and implication of the Foundation
within the Eldercare Centre.

[
26
]

The Court is not asked to adjudicate on the
specific points which have provoked the confrontation.  The Court is asked,
however, to adjudicate upon the rights and obligations of the opposing parties
resulting from their "break‑up" caused by said confrontation.

[
27
]

Around the first part of 1999 the confrontation
became more polarized.  On April 20, 1999, the Unified Board held a meeting at
which the following matters were discussed:

c.
Foundation Matters

Stanley
Selinger stated that he had decided at the last minute to hold the meeting in
camera to allow for a free discussion regarding future fundraising
via the
creation a reconstituted new foundation serving both establishments
.

Two
letters regarding this matter had been sent beforehand to all members to
provide up-dated information regarding on-going discussions.  Stanley Selinger
added that the letters provided but a brief information about all the work done
by him and the officers in this respect and about the progress made.
He
wanted the present meeting to end up by having the members' consensus regarding
a draft resolution that he wished to submit to the executive of the JHH
Foundation as the Board's final proposal towards the creation of a new single
foundation
.  This single foundation would be the unique powerful arm
mandated by the Board to raise funds for non-sharable and other important but
non-funded needs of both establishments, and it would exist in keeping with the
ideology of the foundation's founding fathers and respecting the efforts of the
community at large.

Rather
than entering into lengthy discussions the members agreed to discuss the draft
resolution (copy attached to the official minutes) point by point.  The drafted
resolution was modified as per the attached copy.

M.
Kotler moved to approve the draft resolution as modified during the
discussions, and to submit it to the Officers of the JHH Foundation for
consideration.  G. Weinstein seconded the motion.  Unanimously approved.

The
JNH Foundation has agreed to accept the recommendations of the Board once all
discussions with the JHH Foundation have been concluded
.

The next
steps
necessitate a meeting
by the officers of the JHH Foundation, and
then
a meeting of the JHH Foundation Officers with the Officers of the Board
,
and this prior to May 31, 1999.

(emphasis added)

[
28
]

The following draft resolution was attached:

RESOLUTION FOR A SINGLE FOUNDATION FOR THE JHOH & JNH

WHEREAS:

-

The Jewish Nursing Home and the Jewish Hospital
of Hope are two public establishments which are in the process of concluding a
legal integration as mandated by Bill 120, with a proposed name of Montreal
Jewish Geriatric Center.
[13]

-

These two pubic establishments have been
actively integrating services and management with a view to becoming a single
public establishment, after integration, to be governed by the existing Unified
Board.

-

This Unified Board recognizes the need to have
an ongoing active fund raising program carried out by a single Foundation
dedicated to that purpose.

BE
IT RESOLVED:

1.

That the Unified Board recommends the
establishment of a single Foundation for both Public Establishments and for the
future legally integrated Public Establishment, to raise funds in support of
their objectives and mission.

2.

That this single Foundation be the exclusive
Foundation for future fundraising,
in full support of the establishments'
needs and priorities which are determined by the Unified Board, and which this
foundation is committed to respect and fund
.

3.

That the membership, and directorship of this
Foundation consist of individuals who collectively represent a broad based
community involvement, not originating from a single group or faction, and who
are prepared to engage in active fundraising.

4.

That openness, collaboration and mutual support
characterize the relationship between the Unified Board and this Foundation.

5.

That the Unified Board acknowledges the
negotiations of the officers with the J.H.H. Foundation to reconstitute itself
as the single Foundation, and empowers them to conclude these negotiations, in
respect of articles 1 through 4 of this resolution, by May 31, 1999
.

6.

That the Unified Board acknowledges the
agreement of the J.N.H. Foundation to participate fully in the single
Foundation, either by reconstituting itself or in any other co-operative
manner.  The specifics are to be determined after a conclusion of negotiations
with the J.H.H. Foundation, or the expiry of May 31, 1999 date, whichever comes
first.

7.

That the officers of the Unified Board be
empowered to take the necessary steps to give full force and effect to this
resolution, subject to ratification by the Unified Board.

(emphasis added)

[
29
]

The purpose of the proposed reconstitution was
to create a new relationship between the Eldercare Centre and the Foundation,
where the Foundation would be the Centre's fundraising arm
under the
Eldercare Centre's complete control
.  In the event of a refusal by the
Foundation of the proposal in question, the Nursing Home Foundation would then
be re-organized to fulfil this new function.   The newly reconstituted
Foundation would be reduced to a find‑raising function and the Unified
Board would retain full decision‑making power with respect to the use,
allocation or destination of the funds so collected.  This, the Foundation was
not (and had never been) prepared to accept.

[
30
]

The Foundation did not accept the proposed
resolution because it meant that the Eldercare Centre would henceforth dictate
the "establishment's needs and priorities which are determined by the
Unified Board and which the Foundation is committed to respect and fund".
For the Foundation and its Directors, this amounted to a total abdication in
favour of the views of the members of the Unified Board.   It should be noted
however that at that moment the position of the Unified Board is expressed as
an intention with the hope of convincing the Foundation, and not as a dictate
or an imposition of the wishes of a mandator towards its mandatary.  This will
change with the passage of time and the resistance of the Foundation to fall
under the complete control of the Unified Board.

[
31
]

Negotiations nevertheless continued between the
Eldercare Centre and the Foundation in order to find an acceptable compromise
but, as we will see, to no avail.  On September 6, 2000, some 15 months after
the submission of the draft resolution of May 20, 1999, the following letter is
addressed to the Foundation:

September 6, 2000

JHH
Foundation

5725
Victoria Avenue

Montrea,
Quebec

H3W
3H6

Attention: Mr. Morris Freedman,
President

Dear Mr. Freedman,

As indicated to you at meeting
held on August 30
, attented by Messrs.  Weistein,
Labow, and Sackman, the new Jewish Eldercare Foundation has now hired a
Director to help develop its financial base.  The Foundation will be housed in
the premises now occupied by the JHH Foundation.
As discussed, we are
prepared to help
the transition for the operations of the JHH Foundation to
become part of the Jewish Eldercare Foundation.  The following is
a summary
of the process tabled at our meeting
:

1.

We are prepared to take over your secretarial
position, i.e., Sylvia Rosen, along with all the files pertaining to donor
lists, etc.

2.

We are prepared to allow you, for the present
time, to continue operating the snack bar and gift shop, and we are prepared to
do the accounting and bookkeeping for you.

3.

The JHH Foundation is to cease its operations
and not do any more fundraising
except for its
current campaign, which was started without our knowledge.

4.

All new monies, whether capital or income
shall be paid to the Jewish Edercare Foundation on receipt
.

5.

All income, whether capital, capital gains,
interest, dividends, etc.  shall be payable to the Jewish Edercare Foundation
.

6.

The annual financial statement of the JHH
Foundation must be delivered to us within 120 days of its year-end
.

7.

We intend to publish in appropriate newspapers,
and to notify the community, as well as the legal, accounting, notarial and
insurance professionals
of the phase out of the JNH Foundation and the JHH
Foundation so that all future funds will accrue to the benefit of the Jewish
Eldercare Centre
comprising the former Jewish Hospital of Hope and Jewish
Nursing Home.

Yours truly,

N.
Murray Kotler, FCA

President

(emphasis added)

[
32
]

The receipt of this letter by the Foundation
confirmed, in no unclear terms, that the position of the Eldercare Centre was
definitely set and that its intention was, purely and simply, to force the
Foundation to put an end to its current activities and to be replaced by the
Jewish Eldercare Foundation (In the meantime, the Jewish Nursing Home
Foundation had changed its name to the Jewish Eldercare Foundation and was
becoming the vehicle through which the Eldercare Centre intended to proceed with
its fund-raising plans.  See exhibit P-13.).

[
33
]

There were further attempts to negotiate a new
agreement whereby the Eldercare Centre and the Foundation would be able to
continue to co-exist.  Exhibit P-18 is an example of the last efforts made in
that respect.

[
34
]

At the end of 2000, the Eldercare Centre and the
Foundation are at a complete stand-off.  No agreement could be concluded
between the two institutions over the role and function of the Foundation.  The
boards of the two entities are entrenched in their respective positions.  They
can no longer agree over the funding of the Centre's needs, mainly because they
cannot agree upon which needs are to be funded.

[
35
]

On November 22, 2000, the board of  Directors of
the Foundation, rejected the last draft agreement which could have perhaps
reconciled the parties (Exhibit P-31).

[
36
]

On November 28, 2000, the Foundation (through
its counsel) wrote to the Eldercare Centre informing it of the reasons for its
refusal to ratify the draft agreement P-18.  One of the arguments raised by the
Foundation is that the funds raised through donations could be used by the
Eldercare Centre for purposes other than those permitted by the law governing
charitable organizations, i.e. the payment of salaries, administrative, and
operating expenses.

[
37
]

The situation remained as such over the better
part of the year 2001.  The Foundation continued to raise money through its
various fund-raising activities and campaigns, but against the wishes of the
Eldercare Centre.  When certain needs are identified at the Hospital, the
Foundation spends the money directly towards such needs.  The Foundation
continues however to resist any allocation of its funds by the Eldercare Centre
to cover expenses which, in the Foundation's opinion, should not be covered.

[
38
]

Following a resolution of its Board dated May 2
nd
,
2000, (see Exhibit P-30), on or about May 24, 2001, the Foundation caused the
name "Fondation de l'Hôpital Juif de L'Espérance – Jewish Hospital of Hope
Foundation" to be registered at the "index des noms" of the
Office of the Inspector General of Financial Institutions.
[14]
This registration was effected
after

the Hospital had changed its own corporate name from the Jewish Hospital of
Hope to the "Jewish Eldercare Centre – CHSLD Juif de Montréal (Exhibit P‑15).
Given the fact that the Foundation had always been known as the Jewish Hospital
of Hope Foundation and had operated under such denomination for nearly thirty
years, the Foundation saw no harm in proceeding to register the said name
especially when immediately prior to doing so, the Unified Board had agreed to
re‑name the regroupment of Hospital and the Nursing Home as the Jewish
Eldercare Centre.  This view was not shared by the Plaintiffs.

[
39
]

On July 19, 2001, The Eldercare Centre (through its
counsel) wrote to the Foundation bitterly complaining about the said
registration.  The letter stated in part as follows:

. . .

The Jewish Eldercare
Center (hereinafter "the Center") has been using the name Jewish
Hospital of Hope for over fifty (50) years in connection with the
accomplishment of its purpose namely the serving of the elderly population.
Over
this period of time, the Center has acquired a right of ownership in the name
Jewish Hospital of Hope and has the full and exclusive right to use that name
.
There is significant familiarity by the general public with this name, an
extensive reputation and significant goodwill attached to that name which our
client intends to preserve and which by your conduct, you are injuring.

We understand that on
May
24
th
, 2001, you have registered the name Jewish Hospital of Hope
with the intention of using that name in connection with the activities of the
Foundation
.  You are hereby requested to immediately stop using the name
and take whatever steps are necessary so as to change your name in whatever
fashion necessary so as not to infringe the rights of our client in and to the
name Jewish Hospital of Hope.

. . .

Be furthermore advised by
these presents that
any authorization previously given to you permitting you
to raise money on behalf of the Center is hereby revoked
.  You are not
authorized any longer to solicit any monies on behalf of the Center nor to
associate youselves in any way with the activities of the Center.   Any
activity on your part that will result in a diversion of funds to you as a
result of your associating yourself with the Center is improper and illegal and
you and any persons conspiring with you will be equally held liable in
damages.

Be advised that you are
requested as of October 15
th
, 2001,
to vacate all premises

ANALYSIS

The existence or non‑existence of a contract of
mandate

[
45
]

The Eldercare Centre argues firstly that the
activities of the Foundation, in relation with the Hospital or the Centre
itself, are executed pursuant to a mandate authorizing the Foundation to raise
funds for the benefit of the Hospital.  The termination of this mandate would
therefore preclude the Foundation from engaging into any fund‑raising
activities on behalf of the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre.  The Eldercare

preclude the Foundation from using the full name of the Jewish Hospital of Hope

[
46
]

As indicated in the factual review above, there
is no formal agreement between the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre, and the
Foundation.

[
47
]

If a contract of mandate exists between the two
entities, it can only be a tacit or implicit agreement.

[
48
]

Professor Adrian Popovici
[16]
defines the contract of mandate by
comparing the texts of
articles 2130

C.c.Q.
,  1701 C.C.L.C. and 1984 of the
Code Napoléon.  He writes (at pages 16 and 17 of his treatise):

Le mandat c'est d'abord,
surtout, essentiellement et (vraisemblablement) nécessairement le contrat
défini à l'article 2130:

Le mandat est le contrat par lequel une personne, le
mandant, donne le
pouvoir de la représenter
dans l'accomplissement d'un
acte
juridique

fait de son acceptation,
s'oblige à l'exercer
.

Ce pouvoir et, le cas échéant, l'écrit qui le
constate, s'appellent aussi procuration.

Le C.c.B.C.  de 1866
donnait lui aussi une définition: article 1701:

Le mandat est un contrat par lequel une personne,
qu'on appelle le mandant,
confie la gestion d'un affaire licite
à une
autre personne qu'on appelle mandataire, et qui, par le fait de son
acceptation,
s'oblige à l'exécuter
.  L'acceptation peut s'inférer des
actes du mandataire, et même de son silence en certains cas.

Cette définition ne
coïncidait pas nécessairement avec celle du Code Napoléon de 1884 qui, il faut
le dire, manque un peu de rigueur: article 1984:

Le mandat ou procuration est un
acte
par lequel
une personne donne à une autre le
pouvoir de faire quelque chose
pour le
mandant et en son nom.  Le contrat ne se forme que par
l'acceptation du
mandataire
.

(emphasis added)

[
49
]

He adds (pages 17,18):

Il n'est pas aisé de
différencier, dans certains cas, le mandat d'autres contrats: louage d'ouvrage
ou contrat de service, entreprise, contrat de travail, vente, prêt, dépôt.
L'utilisation du mot "mandat" de façon non scientifique par le
langage de tous les jours ne vient pas faciliter la précision de la pensée.  Le
professeur Fabien écrit avec justesse:

"Mandat" est
[
. . .
]
employé
dans le langage courant pour désigner une tâche quelconque, généralement

qui n'impliquent aucune fonction de représentation, cet usage est à bannir

Malheureusement,
l'utilisation du mot "mandat" à mauvais escient  n'est pas l'apanage
du non‑juriste:  que de "mandats" donnés à un notaire ou même à
un avocat, qui n'en sont pas!

Le mandat donne au
mandataire le pouvoir de le représenter dans un acte juridique avec un tiers.
Sont de l'essence du mandat, il convient de la souligner et de le répéter:

-

le pouvoir de représentation;

-

l'accomplissement d'un acte juridique.

Le pouvoir de
représentation explique l'effet essentiel du mandat:  le mandant est lié par
contrat avec le tiers, de telle sorte que naissent directement dans son
patrimoine des droits et obligations du contrat conclu avec le tiers, avec les
recours réciproques directs contractuels résultant de ce contrat
.  Lorsque
tout fonctionne normalement, le but et l'effet du mandat coïncident.  Qui
mandat ipse fecisse videteur.
[17]

(emphasis added)

[
50
]

Nowhere do we see in the evidence any set of
instructions given at any time to the Foundation by the Hospital.  Nowhere do
we see instructions or even suggestions formulated whereby the Foundation would
oblige itself in any way towards the Hospital.
Article 2138

C.c.Q.
provides
that a mandatary is "bound" i.e. "obligated" to fulfil the
mandate he has accepted.
Article 2139
C.c.Q. also provides for the mandatary's
obligation to report upon the performance of the mandate and
Article 2141

C.c.Q. calls for the obligation of the mandatary to account for its acts.
Nowhere in the evidence do we see facts sustaining such  legal relationship.

[
51
]

The three codified definitions of the contract
of mandate cited above many be slightly different in their wording.  However
all three definitions have two important points in common:  the necessity of an
obligation by the mandatary to execute instructions from the mandator and the
power of the mandatary to bind the mandator (when the mandatary acts within the
terms and conditions of its mandate).  Here, once again, the Court does not see
which instructions the mandatory Foundation has obliged itself to fulfil or
execute on behalf of, or for the account of, the mandator Hospital nor does it
see the power of the Foundation to bind the Hospital in any given situation.

[
52
]

The fact that the Foundation engages itself into
fund‑raising activities
for the benefit of
the Hospital does not
create a relationship of mandator‑mandatary between it and the Hospital.
Nor does it create a relationship of principal‑representative.  Nor does
it permit or authorize the mandatary to bind the mandator, as it would, in a
normal mandate relationship.

[
53
]

Many institutions are involved un fund‑raising.
Such institutions may collect monies for many causes.  A contractual
relationship may be created between the third‑party donor and the donee
Foundation.   The terms and conditions of the gift may oblige the donee to
remit the funds to the recipient Hospital or to such other person or
institution chosen or determined by the donor but this obligation arises from
the terms and conditions of the contract between the third party donor and the
donee and not by reason of a so‑called mandate between the Foundation and
the Hospital.

[
54
]

If, for example, a donor would want to transfer
a substantial amount to the Foundation for the ultimate benefit of the Hospital
but under terms and conditions which would be unacceptable to the Hospital,
surely the Hospital would be entitled to refuse the gift.  But, in this
example, the Foundation would be the mandatary of the donor, not of the
Hospital.

[
55
]

The refusal of the Foundation to the attempt, by
the Hospital, to take control of all fund‑raising activities is not out
of line with its own obligations as a charitable organization.  It should not
be forgotten that such charitable organization benefit from a very important
privilege:
the right to issue tax‑deductible receipts to donors
.
This privilege is entrusted to the Foundation under exceptional (and
restrictively interpretated) provisions of the relevant federal and provincial
income tax legislations.  Such privilege does not come from the Hospital and
creates obligations upon the Foundation which the Foundation is bound to respect
under pain of seeing its tax‑deductible receipts denied by the taxing
authorities or, even more, under pain of seeing its status as a charitable
organization revoked.

[
56
]

This situation obliges the Foundation to
remain independent and to keep at a certain distance from the Hospital
.  This also obliges the Foundation to ensure that the funds
collected are spent and used by the ultimate recipient (in this case, the
Hospital) not only in the manner prescribed by the donor but also within the
confines of what is considered a "charitable purpose" under the
relevant federal and provincial income tax laws and regulations.
[18]

[
57
]

Our Courts are not often called upon to
determine what a charitable organization may or may not do.  Recently, the
Supreme Court of Canada examined the question in
Vancouver Society of
Immigrant and Visible
Minority Women –vs.- M.N.R.
[19]
.  This case arose from the refusal, by
Revenue Canada, to grant to the Applicant Society the appropriate certification
or registration as a charitable organization under ss. 149.1(1) and 248(1) of
the Income Tax Act. (ITA).  Although this case deals more with the question of
whether or not the powers and objects of the Appellant Society qualified as
"charitable purposes" under the ITA (which is not an issue in the
present case), the Court finds in the comments of the Supreme Court some
interesting notions which generally apply to all charitable organizations and
which, if not observed, may bring about either the refusal by Revenue Canada of
a deductible tax receipt or even the de‑certification of the organization
as a charitable organization.
[20]

[
58
]

Mr. Justice Iacobucci in
Vancouver Society

writes as follows (at paragraph 128):

128.

Division H of Part I of the Income Tax Act
("ITA") describes persons who are exempt from tax under Part I.
Included
in this category are, among others, both registered charities and non‑profit
organizations
,  each as defined by the ITA (s. 149(1)(f) and (l),
respectively).  However, a
registered charity is in a more advantageous tax
position even than most other persons listed in Division H:  in addition to the
organization being exempt from tax, contributors to the charity are eligible to
receive tax credits in respect of the contributions made
.  Simple non‑profit
organizations do not enjoy this additional benefit, which is designed to
encourage the funding of activities which are generally regarded as being of
special benefit to society.  That is,
the ability of a charitable
organization to carry out activities in pursuit of its goals often depends on
its ability to attract donations from the public, meaning that the capacity to
offer tax benefits to prospective donors can be a major determinant of the
success of such an organization
.

(emphasis added)

[
59
]

The relevant statutes and regulations do not
define what constitutes a "charitable purpose".  However, the British
and Canadian Courts will not permit a charitable organization to cause the
organization's resources to be used for non‑charitable purposes
[21]
.

[
60
]

Iacobucci, J. adds at paragraphs 142 and 143:

142.

As I have already explained, s. 248(1) of the
ITA empowers the Minister to grant registered‑charity status to qualified
charitable organizations and charitable foundations.  To be considered a
"charitable organization" for the purposes of the ITA, however, an
organization must come within the criteria set out in s 149.1(1), the most
significant of which for the purposes of this appeal is that the organization
must
devote all of its resources to charitable activities
.

143.

While this may appear, at first glance, to be
rather a simple test, it actually poses a number of problems.
For one, the
ITA does not define what is or is not a charitable activity
.  Rather, it
implicitly relies upon the common law for guidance.  As Stone J.A. put it in
Positive Action Against Pornography –vs.- M.N.R., (1988) 2. F.C. 340 (C.A.), at
p. 347:

. . .  the
Act
appears clearly to envisage a resort to
the common law for a definition of "charity" in its legal sense as
well as for the principles that should guide us in applying that definition.

(emphasis added
)

[
61
]

The concept of "charity"  at common‑law
is better defined (amongst other sources) by Lord Macnaghten in
Commissioners
for Special Purposes of the Income Tax –vs.- Pemsel
[22]
as follows:

"Charity in its legal sense
comprises four principal divisions: trusts for the relief of
poverty
:
trusts for the
advancement of education
;  trusts for the
advancement
of religion
; and trusts for
other purposes beneficial to the community
,
not falling under any of the preceding heads.

(emphasis added)

[
62
]

As Mr. Justice Iacobucci explains, the source of
this rather generic definition is found the
Charitable Users Act
of
1601, 43 Elisabeth I c. 4 which states as follows (in its modern English
rendition, as it can be found in the words of Slade J.  in
McGovern –vs.-
Attorney General
[23]
at
page 332):

. . . the relief of aged, impotent
and poor people;  maintenance of sick and maimed soldiers and mariners, schools
of learning, free schools, and scholars in universities;  repair of bridges,
ports, havens, causeways, churches, sea banks and highways; education and
preferment of orphans; relief, stock or maintenance for houses of correction;
marriages of poor maids; supportation, aid and help of young tradesmen,
handicraftsmen and persons decayed; relief or redemption of prisoners or
captives, and for aid or ease of any poor inhabitants concerning payments of
fifteens, setting out of soldiers and other taxes.

[
63
]

While it is not easy to clearly define what a
"charitable purpose" really is and while, as Strayer J. puts it in
Human
Life International in Canada –vs.- M.N.R.
[24]

the definition of charity remains . . . "an area crying out for
clarification through Canadian legislation for the guidance of taxpapers,
administration and the courts", the purpose of this comment is not so much
to attempt to better define the concept but, more importantly, to stress the
importance for a charitable organization to make sure that its activities will
exclusively be charitable.  Iaccobuci J. at paragraph 154:

154.

The final consideration raised by s. 149.1 is
that of
exclusive charitability
.  Under subs. (1), the definition of
"charitable foundation" includes the requirement that it "is
constituted and operated
exclusively for charitable purposes
" and
"charitable organization" means, inter alia, an organization"
all
the resources of which are devoted to charitable activities carried on by the
organization itself
".  The ITA, therefore, clearly
requires that
all of the purposes and activities of the foundation or organization be charitable
.
In light of the preceding discussion regarding the construal of charitable
activities,
exclusively
charitable activities would be those that
directly further charitable purposes and not other, non‑charitable,
purposes.

(emphasis added)

[
64
]

The Court is not asked to review or comment upon
the manner in which the monies collected by the Foundation and used by it or
the Hospital fall within the definition of what is charitable or not under
Canadian or Quebec law.  One thing is clear however:  the definition is far
from being easy to grasp. It is not enough to merely say that medical
assistance is a valid charitable purpose, to conclude that all things done to
provide medical assistance to those who need it will be considered as proper
and legal charitable purposes.  The payment of money to a doctor or a nurse as
an incentive to furnish services or work at the Hospital may be perceived as
necessary and fall within the general definition of charitable purpose.  In
certain instances it may not.  The use of funds collected by the Foundation to
offset deficits is the management and operation of a parking lot may also be
treated differently, depending upon circumstances
[25]
.  The Court expresses no opinion on either
scenario.  The Court re‑emphasizes however the legal necessity for a
Foundation to be independent and at all times capable of exercising proper
control over the funds it collects.  Improper use of those funds may cause
serious problems, for the Foundation itself (loss of certification) or for the
donor (non‑recognition of the tax‑deductible receipt).  In such
instances, it is not the Hospital which would find itself liable towards the
donor.  It is the Foundation.

[
65
]

The necessity for a Foundation to be independent
and to observe all legal requirements imposed to it by law, as this is
illustrated in
Vancouver Society
[26]
,
goes against the notion of implicit or tacit mandate invoked by the
Plaintiffs.  Without an express contract or agreement the Court finds that in
this particular instance, the Plaintiffs have not shown that the Foundations'
activities are governed by any implicit or tacit agreement which, once revoked,
would preclude the Foundation from carrying its fund‑raising activities,
be they for the benefit of the Hospital, the Eldercare Centre or any other
third party.

[
66
]

This does not mean that a formal agreement could
not have intervened between the Hospital and the Foundation, identifying the
rights and obligations of the two institutions and either protecting the
Foundation against any improper use of funds by the Hospital, or allowing the
Foundation to participate into, and agree with, the intended use by the
Hospital of funds collected by, the Foundation.  However no agreement of this
nature has been alleged nor proven.

The exclusivity of the use of the name "Jewish
Hospital of Hope"

[
67
]

The second question to be examined is the
following:  Are the Plaintiffs entitled to the exclusive right to use the name
Jewish Hospital of Hope?

[
68
]

There is no doubt that the name Jewish Hospital
of Hope originally belonged to the corporation of 1942 creating the Hospital.

[
69
]

The Hospital's charter (P-1) confirms that the
name is definitely an asset of the Hospital.  As such, the Hospital may use the
name, in exclusivity, for the purposes and objects of its charter.  The
Hospital may grant the right to use its name to a third party and otherwise
deal with its name in the manner it thinks fit.

[
70
]

But, as we have seen, the Foundation quickly
took the position that it could use the full name Jewish Hospital of Hope
Foundation, from the outset.  Without the fear of causing a direct connection
between the Hospital and the Foundation in 1972 (a situation which was, at the
time, to be avoided at all costs), it may even be presumed that the Foundation
would have been incorporated under the full name rather than under its
abbreviated version.  There is no phonetic or illustrative significance to the
letters J.H.H.  They are somewhat difficult to pronounce and do not suggest any
particular meaning or image
unless
the meaning or image is to suggest
that "J.H.H." stands for "Jewish Hospital of Hope".  In
fact, the Foundation was set up and organized  to be separate and distinct
enough from the Hospital in order to protect its assets and funds.  It was
also

set up to be close enough to be identified as a fund‑raising organization
for the benefit of the Hospital.

[
71
]

Consequently, it can be argued that in the minds
of the incorporators of the Foundation, it was never intended to operate the
Foundation under its abbreviated corporate name composed of a rather
unattractive group of letters.  It was always intended to have the Foundation
operate and be identified as the Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation.  This was
the real purpose.  This is also what happened and what took place in the daily
activities of the Foundation and the Hospital.

[
72
]

As indicated in the factual review above, the
use by the Foundation of the full name Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation was
immediate and constant throughout the period 1972, to the creation of the
Eldercare Centre.  Such use of the full name was not only tolerated by the
Hospital.  It was encouraged.

[
73
]

Such tolerance or encouragement occurred between
the two separate legal entities although they were not bound by any agreement
or even a resolution.  These two legal entities are not linked to each other.
They are (and should be) independent from each other.  There is no
parent-subsidiary relationship between the two corporations (without share‑capital).
There is no legal or conventional set of rights or obligations which link the
two entities other than the fact that, over a period of nearly thirty years,
both entities have worked towards a common goal in relative harmony.

[
74
]

The absence of any contract between the two
entities with respect to the use of the name Jewish Hospital of Hope certainly
causes a major problem to the Plaintiffs.  Although there is no doubt in the
Court's mind that the name originally belonged to the Hospital the question
must be asked:  has the Hospital lost the right to exclusive use of the said
name by reason of its tolerance (or encouragement) in favour of the Foundation?

[
75
]

There is little doctrine and even less case law
on this precise question.  There are numerous cases where conflicting trade
names were expunged from registries or where injunctions were granted stopping
a violator or usurpator of a trade name from unfairly competing with another,
claiming rightful title to the name in question.

[
76
]

Mtre Henri Simon in his book entitled "Le
nom commercial"
[27]

addresses the issue of "Appropriation, Transmission et Perte du Nom
Commercial et de l'Enseigne" as follows:

L'appropriation matérielle
et effective d'un nom commercial
se fait par l'usage.  Aucune protection
n'est accordée pour le simple fait que l'on est le premier à avoir pensé à ce
nom.  L'usage est une condition essentielle à tout appropriation
.
[28]

(emphasis
added)

[
77
]

Clearly, the Foundation has appropriated for
itself (with the blessings of the Hospital) the name Jewish Hospital of Hope as
descriptive words to identify itself.  It has used the name in question without
opposition or challenge by the Hospital for nearly thirty years.

[
78
]

Mtre Simon adds:

Section III:  Perte du nom commercial
et de l'enseigne

A.

FERMETURE DU FONDS

C'est l'hypothèse la plus
ordinaire de perte du droit au nom commercial.
Le fonds de commerce ayant
cessé d'exister le nom commercial devient res nullius
.  La fermeture doit
être définitive.  La fermeture temporaire ne fait pas perdre le droit au nom
commercial.  C'est le cas où le fonds est fermé momentanément à la suite d'un
incendie, d'un décès, pour réparation, pour déménagement ou même pour
difficultés pécuniaires.  Il faut que cette fermeture soit de courte durée car
autrement si la reprise des opérations se fait longtemps après une fermeture
qui semblait définitive, il faudrait accepter que des tiers de bonne foi aient
pu acquérir un droit sur ce nom.

Il faut, d'autre part, que
l'intention
de fermer de façon définitive existe
.  Cette intention pourra être
inférée
des faits
qui entourent la fermeture.

(emphasis added)

[
79
]

Can it be argued that the abandonment of the
name by the Hospital and its replacement by the words "Jewish Eldercare
Centre" would correspond to the notion of permanent closing?  This is what
Mtre Simon has to say:

Le droit au nom commercial
s'acquiert par l'usage.
C'est le non usage qui fait perdre le droit au
nom.  Il faut que l'intention d'abandonner le nom soit le motif qui explique le
non usage
.  Il faut que l'abandon soit effectif et complet.  L'abandon ne
peut être présumé du simple fait que l'on tolère qu'un autre utilise un nom
commercial qui crée un risque de confusion avec celui de premier usager ou que
l'on tarde à poursuivre un usurpateur.
Les éléments habituels d'un abandon
sont le non usage prolongé et l'inaction  à l'égard d'autres usagers du même
nom
.  Cependant, un non usage prolongé non motivé par des circonstances
justifiant cet absence d'usage peut amener à conclure qu'il y a abandon.  Cet
abandon peut s'inférer
lorsqu'un commerçant change son nom commercial
.

L'abandon donne ouverture à
une appropriation même par des concurrents.  Il faudra cependant qu'un délai
suffisant se soit écoulé pour éviter tout risque de confusion entre les deux
commerces.

. . .

Mais si par la tolérance
du premier usager d'autres usurpent un nom commercial
qui crée un risque de
confusion
et que cette usurpation a duré assez longtemps, il y aura non pas
perte du nom mais perte d'un des droits qui y sont rattachés:  le droit
privatif à l'usage du nom
.  Aucun de ces usagers du nom commercial ne peut
empêcher un autre commerçant, même s'il s'établit postérieurement, d'utiliser
le nom pour désigner un commerce similaire.
Il n'y a plus de droit exclusif
à l'usage de ce nom commercial
.
[29]

(emphasis added)

80

Marks and Unfair Competition
[30]
writes
the following (at page 280):
