The exclusive right to the user of a trade mark may be in any one of the
following cases:

1.

Abandonment.

2.

Loss of distinctiveness by

(a)

Improper assignment;

(b)

Improper licensing;

(c)

Common user of the mark;

(d)

The expiration of a patent on an article in
association with which a trade mark has been used.

3.

Fraud.

4.

removal from the Register.

ABANDONMENT

Trade
mark rights, like any other right, may be the lost by abandonment.  In the case
of a registered trade mark the registration becomes invalid if
the trade
mark has been abandoned
.

(emphasis added)

[
81
]

Then, at page 281:

Intention:  If, of course, as well
as discontinuing to deal in the goods in question, the
proprietor of the
mark ceases to have any intention of dealing in the goods, that would entail an
abandonment of the mark
.  An intention to abandon may be inferred from long
disuse.  So also, the
adoption of new marks may show an intention to abandon
an older and unused mark, but such is not conclusive.  The test is one of
reputation based upon user;  mere intention to preserve the name or mark is not
sufficient
.

Where a trade mark owner
stands
by and allows wide‑spread infringement to go unchecked
, the court may
presume an intention on his part to
abandon his exclusive rights in his mark
.
But an intention to abandon may not always be proved by neglect to proceed in
respect of infringement.  It may be implied from conduct indicating that the
trade mark owner intended the mark to fall into the public domain, thus
causing
an estoppel against the assertion of exclusive rights
in the mark.
Abandonment
is in each case a question of fact, to be determined according to the
circumstances of each particular case and depending on the evidence of
intention to abandon
.  A man will not be held to have abandoned his rights
unless
the court comes to the conclusion that he intended to do so
.

(emphasis added)

[
82
]

The foregoing suggests that the entire issue of
a abandonment or loss of exclusivity in the use of a name or mark is
essentially a question of fact left to the appreciation of the Court.

[
83
]

The Court is of the opinion that, in the present
circumstances, the Hospital, by its tolerance and encouragement towards the use
of the full name Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation by the Foundation, by its
own abandonment of its former corporate name (from the Jewish Hospital of Hope
to the Jewish Eldercare Centre) and by its intent to eventually change the name
of the Hospital of Hope Pavilion to another name (presumably the name of a
donor), has lost its
exclusive
right to the use of the words
"Jewish Hospital of Hope".  Consequently an injunction prohibiting
such use by the Foundation does not lie and cannot be granted.

[
84
]

In addition, the Foundation has been allowed to
function as the Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation for nearly thirty years
without a formal agreement with respect to the use of the said name.  To prohibit
the same organization from continuing the same activities within the same
community under the name under which it has always be known appears to be
contrary to common sense.  If, as it is shown in the analysis of the previous
question,
there is no implicit or tacit mandate (or other type of contract)

between the Hospital and the Foundation, then the tolerance and encouragement
of the Hospital towards the use of the full name, amounts to acquiescence.
Thirty years is too long a delay to claim an exclusivity which was never
enforced.  It is not because the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre have decided
that henceforth the alleged "mandate" previously given or the
"authorization" previously granted are revoked, that the Foundation must
comply and stop from being called what it has been called for nearly three
decades.  No evidence of such mandate or authorization has been made with any
sufficient preponderance to sustain this approach.

[
85
]

It follows that the Hospital (the Eldercare
Centre) has lost its right to enforce any exclusive right towards the name that
the registration of the name by the Foundation is not inappropriate and does
not violate any of the rights of the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre.

[
86
]

It follows also that the continuation of the use
of the name by the Foundation is not likely to cause any confusion with the
Jewish Eldercare Centre or the Jewish Eldercare Foundation.   Firstly,
confusion can be envisaged only when there is an unauthorized use.  Secondly,
the two institutions now have different names.

[
87
]

Finally, the Court is unable to find any legal
basis to condemn the Directors to exemplary damages for having acted in bad
faith or having secretly conspired to deprive the Hospital or the Eldercare
Centre of its name.  The Directors simply acted to confirm a factual situation
which had prevailed for a very long time.  The Court cannot see how the
Directors can be blamed for their acts after the Hospital had itself agreed to
be henceforth called the Jewish Eldercare Centre.   In any event, as indicated
before, the Plaintiffs were not inclined to insist further on this aspect of
their recourse.

[
88
]

The conclusions of the action also seek
conclusions enjoining the Foundation from using or disbursing any of the monies
received for the benefit of the Hospital and to reimburse the Hospital and/or
the Eldercare Centre all such funds received.  While it is true that the
Hospital and/or the Eldercare Centre, are generally entitled to receive the
benefit of donations collected by the Foundation, it does not mean that the
Plaintiffs are automatically entitled to permanent injunctive relief along
those lines.  No evidence was adduced suggesting, let alone demonstrating, that
this would not be the case.  Before, such injunction is granted or even
considered, some evidence of the Foundation's conduct, contrary to its
obligations towards the donors with, which, with or whom it has contracted, is
necessary.   To the contrary, the evidence tends to show that the Foundation
has always used the funds it has received in accordance with the wishes of the
donors or in accordance with its obligations as a charitable organization.
There may have been some instances where the Foundation did not agree with the
Hospital's intended use of the funds but not to a point where the Foundation
would have violated its obligations.  Finally, in case of conflicts or
differences of views on the "charitable purpose" of the intended use
of such funds, the Foundation must be the organization which has final decision‑making
power with respect to the use of the funds it collects.  It is the Foundation,
not the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre which engages its liability towards
third party donors, through the issuance of tax‑deductible receipts.

[
89
]

For all of the foregoing reasons, the principal
action cannot succeed.

THE CROSS-DEMAND

[
90
]

The Foundation and its Directors are seeking two
different conclusions by way of their cross‑demand.  The first conclusion
sought is in the style of a declaratory judgment declaring "
ultra vires
"
and null the "decision" of September 6, 2000, of the chairman of the
board of the Eldercare Centre as being contrary to the
Loi sur la santé et
les services sociaux
, the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Liberties

and the
Charte Québécoise des droits et libertés de la personne
.  The
second conclusion sought is an order enjoining the Eldercare Centre and the
Eldercare foundation to cease and desist from any action which may cause the
public to believe that the Foundation is to disappear and be replaced by the
Jewish Eldercare Foundation.  Let us look at these two propositions
separately.

THE DECLATORY CONCLUSION

[
91
]

The Foundation seeks a declaration that the
letter of September 6, 2000, is for all intents and purposes, unenforceable.
This letter is reproduced in full in paragraph [31] "supra".  A
careful reading of the text of this letter reveals the following:

a)

firstly, the letter appears to summarize what
has occurred at a meeting held on August 30;

b)

secondly, the letter appears to summarize what
was either discussed or communicated by the representatives of the Eldercare
Centre to the representatives of the Foundation and proceeds to enumerate . . .
" a summary of the process tabled at our meeting."

c)

thirdly, a list of seven points which
essentially contain the position of the Eldercare Centre.

[
92
]

The letter in question is no more and no less
than the written summary of a position taken by the Eldercare Foundation.  It
is a negotiating position.   Furthermore the evidence shows that negotiations
continued between the parties after September 6, 2000, and the institution of
the present recourse.  Finally, the conclusions sought by the Plaintiffs
differ, in some respects, from what was proposed in the letter in question.

[
93
]

Article 453 of the Code of Civil Procedure indicates
the context within which a declaratory judgment may be sought:

453.

Celui qui a intérêt à faire déterminer immédiatement, pour la solution d'une
difficulté réelle, soit en son état, soit quelque droit, pouvoir ou
obligation pouvant lui résulter d'un contrat,
d'un testament ou de tout
autre écrit instrumentaire
, d'une loi, d'un arrêté en conseil, d'un
règlement ou d'une résolution d'une municipalité, peut, par requête au
tribunal, demander un jugement déclaratoire à cet effet.

453.
Any person who has an interest in having determined immediately,
for the solution of a genuine problem, either his status or any right, power
or obligation which he may have under a contract,
will or any other
written instrument
, statute, order in council, or resolution or by-law of
a municipality, may, by motion to the court, ask for a declaratory judgment
in that regard.

[
94
]

Can it said that the letter of September
6,constitutes a "contract,
will or any other written instrument
,
statute, order in council or resolution or by-law . . ."?  The only
possible category which may be envisaged here is the one which refers to
"wills or any other written instrument".  The
French text speaks of "d'un testament ou de tout autre écrit
instrumentaire".

[
95
]

It is well settled in Quebec law that Courts are
not available to give legal opinions to the parties before them unless such
opinion is necessary to put an end to a dispute.
[31]
Otherwise, the system would quickly
become over-saturated with such motions.

[
96
]

This is why art. 453 C.C.P.  has limited the
type of documents which may be submitted to the Court for the purpose of
obtaining a declaratory judgment.  These documents must be limited to those
which create or impose rights or obligations upon the parties.  A simple letter
stating a position taken by party "A" vis‑à‑vis party
"B" may not fall into scope of art. 453 C.C.P.

[
97
]

A careful reading of this article indicates that
the words "written instrument" do not stand alone.  They are coupled
to the word "will" in the sentence "will or other written
instrument".  Ordinary grammatical construction suggests therefore that
the kind of "written instrument" envisaged is a document in the
nature of a will.  That is to say a unilateral document which grants certain
rights to a third party.  For example, a donation.

[
98
]

The
Shorter Oxford English Dictionary
[32]
defines the word "instrument"
when used un a legal context, as:

"A
formal
legal
document whereby a right is
created
or
confirmed
or a fact
recorded
;
a formal writing of any kind as an agreement, deed, charter or record drawn up
and executed in technical form."

[
99
]

The
Merriam‑Webster' Collegiate
Dictionary
[33]

defines the same word as follows:

"Middle English, from Latin
Instrumentum . . . a formal legal document."

[
100
]

The French expression "autre écrit instrumentaire"
invites us to look at the definition of the word "instrumentaire".
Le Nouveau Petit Robert
[34]
:

"Instrumentaire: - témoin
instrumentaire, qui assiste un officier ministériel dans les actes dont la
validité requiert la présence de témoins."

[
101
]

The notion of "écrit instrumentaire"  includes the
necessity of a certain formalism to the written document which is to be
interpreted by the Court in the process of a declaratory judgment.  So also for
the notion of "written instrument".  A mere letter summarizing what
was discussed at a meeting does not fall within either the French or the
English ordinary sense given to these words.  To decide otherwise would then
open the recourse envisaged by article 453 C.C.P. to all mises-en-demeure, notices
or other written communications addressed to an adverse party in the context of
negotiation or litigation.  The judicial system would then become a testing
ground for strategic positions or arguments for purposes of negotiation.  This
is neither the purpose nor the "raison d'être" of article 453 C.C.P.

[
102
]

Consequently the Court is of the opinion that the procedure of
declaratory judgment does not apply to the letter of September 6, 2000, because
such letter is not an "écrit instrumentaire" or a "written instrument"
as these words are used in article 453  C.C.P.

[
103
]

The Defendant Foundation is not unaware of this problem.  Its
conclusion is carefully drafted and refers to the letter of September 6 as a
"decision" in an attempt to give to the said letter a formality or an
appearance of binding effect which does not exist in the present
circumstances.

[
104
]

Even if the contents of the letter would have been copied from the
text of a formal resolution of the board of directors of the Eldercare Centre
(which it is not) this would still remain, in the context of this instance a
statement of position by a party towards another, in the context of a legal
conflict (whether immediate or eventual).  It would still not be a
"written instrument" within the meaning to be given to these words in
article 453 C.C.P.

[
105
]

It should also be noted that the said letter is dated September 6,
2000 whilst the injunction proceedings of the Plaintiffs are dated August 22
nd
,
2001, nearly one year later.  During that period, the respective positions of
the Foundation and of the Eldercare Centre continued to change an evolve
towards other proposals or counter‑proposals.  When the Plaintiffs
decided to institute their injunction proceedings, they did not attempt to
enjoin the Defendant Foundation with a position identical to what was alleged
in the letter of September 6, 2001.  Their injunctive relief sought only
matters concerning the
use of the name in the activities of the Foundation

or concerning
the accounting of funds collected for the benefit of the
Hospital
. If the letter of September 6 had been an "écrit
instrumentaire" or a "written instrument", the injunctive relief
would have had to include a verbatim rendition of the contents of the said
letter.

[
106
]

Notwithstanding the Court's conclusion with respect to the non‑application
of article 453 C.C.P. to the said letter, could it be reasonably argued that
the contents of the letter could be "
ultra-vires
" the powers
of the Eledercare Centre or violate the Foundation's rights under the Canadian
or Quebec Charters?  Although the Court chooses not to formally opine on these
issues, it would seem, if it were to so opine, that nothing in the said letter
is so illegal or unenforceable that it would require a declaration of
illegality or unenforceability.    There is nothing fundamentally wrong or
illegal in the position advanced by the Eldercare Centre in the letter of
September 6, 2000.  Each of the issues raised could be negotiated, improved and
made acceptable to both parties.  While certain statements may go too far
towards the control of funds raised by the Foundation, it is not impossible to
consider a situation where proper assurances would be given so as to ensure the
improper dedication of such funds towards activities or uses which are
perfectly acceptable as "charitable purposes".  In other words, the
said letter may have been unacceptable as it was originally drafted.  It could
have been improved with further discussions and concessions from both sides.
This was not done to the satisfaction of both sides.  There was no deal or
settlement reached on the proposal advanced by the Eldercare Centre.  That is
all.

[
107
]

The Court has dealt with what the Eldercare Centre has attempted to
enforce.  Nothing further needs to be said with respect of the contents of the
letter of September  6, 2000.

[
108
]

Consequently, the Foundation's conclusion for a declaratory judgment
will be dismissed.

THE FOUNDATION'S INJUNCTIVE
RELIEF

[
109
]

Can the Foundation stop or enjoin the Eldercare Centre and its newly
re‑organized Eldercare Foundation from representing to the public in
general that the Foundation will or may disappear and be replaced by the
Eldercare Foundation?

[
110
]

Two issues must be analyzed here:  the disappearance of the
Foundation and the replacement of the Foundation on the one hand and the
replacement of the Foundation as the primary fund‑raiser of the Eldercare
Foundation, on the other hand.

[
111
]

There is no threat by the Eldercare Centre to cause the
disappearance

of the Foundation.  Before this Court, the Eldercare Centre recognizes the
existence of the Foundation and argues that the Foundation is totally free to
continue to act, function and raise funds, as long as it remains identified as
the J.H.H. Foundation.  The Court has already decided that the Foundation could
continue to use its full denomination of the Jewish Hospital of Hope
Foundation, as it has always been known for the last thirty years.  Nothing
further needs to be added.  There is no allegation or intent by the Eldercare
Centre to cause the disappearance of the Foundation as an organization.  No
injunctive relief is necessary.  There is no peril in this respect.  No threat
along those lines was either alleged nor proven.

[
112
]

Consequently,  the Court will not grant the order sought.

[
113
]

Can the Foundation be "replaced" by the Jewish Eldercare
Foundation?

[
114
]

The Hospital and the Nursing Home have now become unified and are
operated under the name Jewish Eldercare Centre.  In the mind of the members of
the board of directors of the Eldercare Centre, there is little or no advantage
in continuing to raise funds for the benefit of the Eldercare Centre through
the vehicle of foundations which will continue to make reference to the Jewish
Nursing Home or the Jewish Hospital of Hope.  As a result, the Eldercare Centre
has invited the Foundation to become the Jewish Eldercare Foundation.  The
Foundation has declined the invitation and has elected to continue to operate
under its name.  This is its prerogative.  There is nothing which the Eldercare
Centre may do about it.  However, the Eldercare Centre has invited the Nursing
Home Foundation to become its principal fund‑raising arm, in the event of
the Foundation's refusal.  The Nursing Home Foundation has accepted and has
caused its name to be changed to become known as the Eldercare Foundation.  It
may or may not have all of the powers or objects to function adequately
[35]
but if it does not, it can easily be
corrected through the obtention of an appropriate amended certificate of
incorporation.  But, the issue raised by the Foundation goes beyond the
question of the present powers and objects of the Jewish Eldercare Foundation.
It goes to the right of the Eldercare Foundation to create a new fund‑raising
institution.

[
115
]

An answer to the question is found in the following provisions of
the
Loi sur les services de santé et les services sociaux
[36]
.

[
116
]

Section 129
, to
132.1
of the
Act
determines the composition of the
boards of directors of the various types of establishments to which the Act
applies, which included a "CHSLD".  More particularly section 132
would seem to apply to the Eldercare Center.  It reads as follows:

132.

Le conseil d'administration d'un établissement qui
exploite un centre hospitalier ou d'un établissement qui exploite à la fois un
centre d'hébergement et de soins de longue durée et un centre hospitalier de
soins généraux et spécialisés de 50 lits ou plus est composé des personnes
suivantes qui en font partie au fur et à mesure de leur élection ou nomination:

1.

quatre personnes élues par la population lors de
l'élection tenue en vertu de l'article 135

2.

une personne élue par et parmi les médecins,
dentistes et pharmaciens qui exercent leur profession dans tout centre exploité
par l'établissement, une personne élue par et parmi les infirmières et
infirmiers qui travaillent pou l'établissement, une personne élue par et parmi
les personnes membres du conseil multidisciplinaire, y compris les personnes
qui exercent pour l'établissement des activités d'infirmières et infirmiers
auxiliaires, et une personne élue par et parmi les autres personnes qui
travaillent pour l'établissement;

3.

le cas échéant, deux personnes nommées par le
comité des usagers de l'établissement;

4.

trois personnes nommées par les membres de la
personne morale, lorsque l'établissement est une personne morale désignée par
le ministre en vertu de l'article 139;

5.

le cas échéant, une personne ou, si le
paragraphe 4 ne trouve pas application, deux personnes nommées par le conseil
d'administration de la fondation de l'établissement ou, s'il existe plus d'une
fondation pour l'établissement, élues conjointement par les conseils
d'administration de ces fondations
;

6.

le directeur général de l'établissement;

7.

quatre personnes nommées par les membres visés aux
paragraphes 1 et 3 à 5.

1991, c. 42, a. 132;
1996, c. 36,
a.8
,
1998, c.39, a 48
.

(emphasis added)

[
117
]

Section 132(5) points to the possibility of having more than one
foundation for an establishment such as the Eldercare Centre.  In point of
fact, the
Act
provides for the same possibility of multiple foundations for
other establishments to which the said Act applies.  See for example
sections
129(5)
,
130(5)
,
131(4)
,
131.1(5)
and
132.1(5)
of the Act.

[
118
]

Section 132.2
of the
Act
reads as follows:

132.2.

Pour l'application du paragraphe 5 de chacun des articles 129, 130,
131.1, 132 et 132.1 ou du paragraphe 4 de l'article 131, on entend par
"fondation d'un établissement" une personne morale constituée à des
fins non lucratives et ayant essentiellement pour objet de recueillir les
contributions verses en faveur d'un établissement résultant de la fusion ou de
la conversion de cet établissement ou ayant principalement pour objet de
recueillir des contributions devant être utilisées, pour une ou des fins
correspondant à celles mentionnées à l'article 272
[37]
, au
bénéfice de tout ou partie de la mission poursuivie par un tel établissement.

1998 c.39, a.50
.

[
119
]

Nowhere in the
Act
do we see the concept of
only one foundation
for one establishment
.  On the contrary, there can be as many foundations
as the necessities will bear.  The Act specifically provides that an
establishment may have on (or more) foundations engaged in fund‑raising
activities for its benefit.  However, to be considered as a "fondation
d'un établissement" within the purview of the Act, and to be represented
on the board of an establishment (namely pursuant to sect. 132(5) of the Act) a
foundation must make sure that the name of the establishment is specifically
designated in the charter or "acte constitutif"  of the Foundation in
question.

[
120
]

The Charter of the Foundation does not refer specifically to either
the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre.  Nor, for that matter, the Charter of the
Nursing Home Foundation.

[
121
]

Consequently, the Foundation is not and has never been the
foundation of the newly formed establishment called the Jewish Eldercare
Centre.  Inasmuch as the
Act
applied to the Hospital prior to the unification
or prior to the creations of the Eldercare Center, it could not be argued that
the Foundation was the "fondation de l'établissement" then known as
the Jewish Hospital of Hope, at least for the purposes of
section 132
of the
Act.  It did not stop the Foundation from acting as if it was or the Hospital
from approving or encouraging the Foundation to represent itself as being the
Foundation of the Jewish Hospital of Hope.  But this did not create
any
exclusive right
for the Foundation to be considered as the
only

foundation engaged in fund‑raising for the Hospital or for the Eldercare
Centre.

[
122
]

Consequently, the Court sees no legal basis which would permit the
Foundation to assert a right which would justify an  order of permanent
injunction prohibiting its replacement by the Jewish Eldercare Foundation.
The Foundation is not replaced.  A new foundation in entering into the
picture.  The two organizations are entitled to exist in the pursuit of their
respective goals.

CONCLUSION

[
123
]

The Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation will therefore be able to
continue its activities.  So also for the Jewish Eldercare Foundation.  Both
Foundations will solicit the same community of potential donors.  The funds
collected will eventually find their way into the Eldercare Centre as a whole
or into what used to be the Hospital if the Eldercare Centre wishes to accept
the funds so donated.  There may be some lack of efficiency in the process or
some better way to organize and pool resources.  But this is not what the Court
is asked to decide.  Efficiency and proper organization depends not upon orders
of the Court but upon the good will of all involved in the pursuit of the
common goal or common objective as stated in paragraph [1] of this judgment.

[
124
]

The Foundation may continue to use the name Jewish Hospital of Hope
Foundation if it believes there is merit in pursuing this approach.  It may
continue to raise funds using the said name if it believes that members of the
community will want to continue to support the institution by continuing to use
the Hospital's name.

[
125
]

It is not for the Court to suggest how or through which calling the
funds are to be collected with the better chance of success.

[
126
]

The Foundation may operate
a
gift shop or
a
coffee
shop
under the name
Jewish Hospital of Hope Foundation.  However the
Court expresses no opinion as to the Foundation's right to occupy premises
within the Eldercare Centre for such purposes.  This results from whatever
occupation arrangements may exist between the Hospital or the Eldercare Centre
as lesser, and the Foundation as lessee.  This Court is not seized of the
question of determining such relationship between the parties.  In point of
fact, this issue is apparently being debated in separate legal proceedings
before another tribunal.

[
127
]

It has not been shown that the Foundation has used or distributed
any monies received from third‑party donors for any purposes other than
those for which the Foundation has received the funds in question.  Once again
the Court does not say that the Foundation is not obliged to respect the
conditions under which it accepts a gift or bequest from a third party.  It
only states that there is no need to grant injunctive relief imposing a
procedure of accounting under pain of contempt of Court, if not followed,
given the facts proven in this case.

[
128
]

Hopefully the parties to this litigation will find a proper and
harmonious way to work together if the way they presently pursue is not.  They
will, however, have to find this better way themselves.

[
129
]

There will be no order as to costs, given the nature of the case,
the mitigated result and, more particularly, the fact that the resources of the
parties should be put to much better use.

[
130
]

, the
Court:

DISMISSES
the Plaintiffs' action.

DISMISSES
the Defendant's cross-demand.

272.

Un établissement public peut accepter l'aide financière ou matérielle
de toute fondation ou de toute personne morale qui sollicite du public le
versement de sommes ou de dons dans le domaine de la santé ou des services
sociaux pour l'une ou l'autre des fins suivantes:

1.

l'achat, la construction, la rénovation, l'amélioration,
l'agrandissement ou l'aménagement de biens immobiliers de l'établissement;

2.

l'achat, l'installation, l'amélioration ou le remplacement de
l'ameublement, de l'équipement ou de l'outillage de l'établissement;

3.

les activités de recherche de l'établissement;

4.

l'amélioration de la qualité de vie des usagers de l'établissement;

5.

la formation et le développement des ressources humaines de
l'établissement pour des besoins spécifiques.

Avant d'accepter une telle aide, l'établissement doit soumettre son
projet à la régie régionale pour évaluation et acceptation dans les cas
suivants:

1.

lorsque l'aide vise le financement d'un projet pour la réalisation
duquel l'autorisation préalable du Conseil du trésor, du ministre ou de la
régie régionale est requise par la présente loi;

2.

lorsque le projet envisagé a pour effet immédiat ou prévisible
d'augmenter le montant des dépenses annuelles de fonctionnement ou
d'immobilisation de l'établissement;

3.

lorsque, indépendamment du montant de l'aide, l'utilisation recherchée
ne s'inscrit pas à l'intérieur des activités prévues de l'établissement dans
les plans régionaux d'organisation de services élaborés par la régie régionale;

4.

(paragraphe abrogé).

La demande doit être accompagnée des documents et contenir les
renseignements que la régie régionale détermine.

Après avoir évalué la pertinence et la viabilité financière du projet
et après s'être assurée que la fondation ou la personne morale présente des
perspectives financières lui permettant de respecter ses engagements, la
régionale avise l'établissement de l'admissibilité de son projet ou des
conditions requises pour qu'il puisse être accepté.

La régie régionale ne peut toutefois accepter un projet visé au
paragraphe 2 du deuxième alinéa que si l'établissement démontre que les coûts
supplémentaires peuvent être supportés sans requérir d'ajustement budgétaire ou
de subvention particulière de la part de la régionale ou du ministre.

273.

La régie régionale peut, à tout moment, vérifier l'exactitude des
renseignements que lui a fournis l'établissement relativement à un projet
soumis suivant l'article 272 ou requérir tout renseignement sur l'utilisation
de l'aide obtenue conformément à cet article, le cas échéant.

Si l'établissement a obtenu le droit de bénéficier de l'aide au moyen
de fausses représentations ou s'il a employé toute partie de cette aide à
d'autres fins que celles pour lesquelles elle devait être utilisée, la régie
régionale peut, d'office ou à la demande du ministre, déclarer l'établissement
déchu du bénéfice de l'aide accordée et prendre toute mesure pour obliger
l'établissement et la fondation ou personne morale qui verse l'aide à rectifier
la situation.
